title: multi-arch-kv-cache-bottleneck-writeup
content:
Purpose and scope:
This note captures experiment logs and hypotheses from a focused investigation into a recurring latency pattern we see across three representative model families (LLaMA-derived dense, Mistral-like narrow FFN variants, and Qwen-style transformer) when operating with long contexts and our prefix/KV cache enabled. We also include observations for a small MoE routing workload to isolate routing overheads. The goal: figure out where time is being spent on cache-hit requests vs. cold-start requests and produce actionable mitigations that avoid changes to model code paths where possible.

High-level summary (TL;DR):
- KV/prefix cache hits reduce compute substantially but uncover several non-GPU bottlenecks: memcpy and CPU-side router/kernel-launch overheads dominate in mid- to long-context scenarios.
- Mistral-like models (wider attention + smaller FFN) show higher kernel launch density (more smaller kernels) which amplifies GPU launch overheads; batching helps but latency SLOs suffer for single-request workloads.
- Qwen-style models with rotary/ALiBi and long contexts incur extra memory traffic in KV build/consume; cache format (interleaved vs contiguous) matters for GPU memcpy and kernel read efficiency.
- MoE routing cost is primarily CPU/host-side for our current CPU router implementation; moving router to GPU or offloading with a fused kernel reduces latency by ~18–30% in our tests.

Testbed and configuration:
- HW: p4d-equivalent (8xA100/40GB) for scale tests, single A100-40GB for microbenchmarks. Hosts: c6i.4xlarge-like for routing/CPU tests.
- Serving runtime: branch perf/kv-cache-2025 (continuous batching off for baseline single-request latency).
- Models: llama-13b-dense-8bit, mistral-7b-fused-ffn-8bit, qwen-7b-rotary-8bit (all quantized to 8-bit activation paths used for parity with production settings).
- Workloads: single request generate 512 tokens with 2k prefix (cache hit vs cold), and streaming generation to 2048 tokens (prefix grows).
- Measurement: median/95p latencies from 100 warm runs, nvprof/nvtx spans + cpu perf counters, and host-side flamegraphs for router threads.

Representative microbenchmarks (median latencies, single A100):
- Cold-start 512 tokens (no cache): llama-13b: 280ms; mistral-7b: 230ms; qwen-7b: 260ms.
- Cache-hit 512 tokens (prefix in-memory, KV hit): llama-13b: 95ms; mistral-7b: 120ms; qwen-7b: 110ms.
- Streaming to 2048 tokens (cache accumulating): llama-13b: 700ms; mistral-7b: 760ms; qwen-7b: 720ms.
- MoE routing baseline (2k prefix, 512 gen): 340ms (router on CPU). Offload router+fused kernel: 270ms.

Key observations and traces:
1) Host-side memcpy + pinned memory sync spikes on cache-hit paths
- nvprof timelines show that after the initial KV read, the GPU idles while host memcpy and cudaMemcpyAsync -> stream synchronize happen. For cache-hit, time between subsequent token kernels is dominated by small memcpy chunks (~200–400KB per token step depending on KV layout).
- Impact: ~30–40ms added latency per single-token batch in single-request mode.
- Hypothesis: our current KV layout stores keys/values interleaved per layer leading to many small contiguous copies. Contiguous per-layer slabs reduce number of memcpy ops.

2) Kernel launch overhead and many small kernels (Mistral case)
- Mistral-style fused attention has smaller FFNs but higher kernel count per step. Each kernel launch for small payloads (short sequences / cached KV) has fixed latency ~5–8ms. The aggregate adds up.
- Experiment: fused-kernel path (experimental) reduced number of kernels by ~40% and reduced cache-hit latency for mistral by ~18ms (15%).

3) KV cache format matters for Qwen long-context throughput
- Qwen's rotary/projection layout increases per-head KV stride; when cache stored per-token contiguous it caused more page faults and TLB churn. Switching to per-layer contiguous slab improved memcpy throughput by ~22%.
- For long-context workloads (prefix > 4k tokens), we see GPU memory bandwidth become critical: we observe read amplification on layers with large head counts.

4) MoE router CPU overhead and thread contention
- Router currently executes on host CPU, computes gating weights and top-k expert selection, then issues scatter/gather to GPU. This sequence serializes with host->device copies and stream synchronization causing visible stalls.
- Flamegraphs show top CPU time spent in softmax+topk on a single thread; multithreading reduces wall time but increases lock contention and scheduling jitter under load.
- Offloading the softmax/topk to a CUDA kernel (fused routing) reduced end-to-end by 18–30% depending on batch size.

5) Small-batch scheduling vs large-batch throughput tradeoffs
- Continuous batching helps throughput but hurts single-request latency when we add queueing delay. For edge SLOs (<=100ms), small-batch path must avoid extra kernel launches or host syncs.
- Suggestion: introduce a low-latency fast-path that prioritizes colocated KV slab layout + pre-allocated pinned buffers to avoid memcpy setups for single-request cache hits.

Actionable mitigations (short-term):
- Reformat KV cache to per-layer contiguous slabs. Benchmarks above show this reduces memcpy ops by ~60% and improved latency ~12–20% for cache-hit paths. (PR: perf/kv-slab-layout in review).
- Introduce pinned-buffer pool per worker to amortize cudaMemcpyAsync overhead (hotfix branch: pinned-pool-2026).
- Add an experimental fused kernel for Mistral FFN+attention that reduces kernel count; enable behind runtime flag to A/B test.
- Prototype GPU-side routing kernel for MoE; move gating+topk into a single CUDA launch where feasible. (Tickets: INF-1223, INF-1298).

Actionable mitigations (mid-term):
- Revisit KV caching format end-to-end: support two operational formats (low-latency per-layer slab + high-throughput interleaved) selectable by model and workload type.
- Kernel fusion roadmap: target a merged attention+ffn baseline for families that exhibit high kernel density (Mistral variants). This ties into our compiler/kernel-selection layer.
- Adaptive batching: runtime should detect cache-hit, single-request patterns and opt into the low-latency path with reserved pinned buffers and pre-warmed CUDA streams.

Open questions / follow-ups:
- How much of the memcpy+sync overhead is CUDA driver behavior? We should test with newer driver stacks (test matrix: cu117 vs cu121 equivalent).
- Qwen long-context: is the attention implementation (we use a custom rotary allocator) adding additional reads? Need layer-level nvprof traces with memory access pattern analysis.
- MoE quality tradeoffs for fused routing: does a GPU routing kernel numerically match CPU topk with same FP quantization? Need regression evals.

Notes / raw trace excerpts (trimmed):
- nvprof snippet (cache-hit step 87)
  attention_fwd_kernel  12.3ms
  ffn_part1_kernel       5.8ms
  memcpy H2D slab        7.4ms  (multiple small memcpy calls)
  next_token_kernel      10.0ms
  idle/wait              18.6ms  (host sync + stream sync)

- cpu flame (router thread) top stack frames:
  softmax_forward -> topk_select -> std::nth_element -> dispatch_expert -> memcpy_to_device
  (softmax+topk ~ 42% of router time in single-thread baseline)

Recommended immediate priorities (owner: eng-serving-runtime)
1) Merge KV slab layout PR and A/B test across LLaMA/Mistral/Qwen canaries. Timeline 2 weeks.
2) Land pinned-buffer pool as emergency mitigation for cache-hit latency. Timeline 1 week.
3) Start prototype GPU router (research spike) and run numeric parity tests vs CPU routing. Timeline 3 weeks.

Misc: links / references / tickets
- Linear INF-1223 (MoE GPU routing spike), INF-1298 (KV cache slab work)
- Slack: #perf-kv-cache thread (link pinned in Linear INF-1223)
- PR: github.com/redwood-inference/serving-runtime/pull/987 (pinned-buffer pool prototype)

TODOs (for next edits):
- Add full nvprof + Nsight capture attachments (large) — store in shared drive folder /artifacts.
- Run parity evals on Qwen rotary path with 8k context and capture memory page-faults.
- Bake these optimizations into Dedicated capacity sizing doc (estimate cost impact vs throughput improvements).

Notes to reviewers: this is a working doc. numbers are from lab runs and may vary by driver and packing. If you run the attached microbench harness, please add logs to the INF tickets.

Signed: Aisha (on behalf of eng-serving-runtime perf subteam)
